toc.title: But you don't need to know the cause
Reframe fixing into validate, normalize, permit

blocks.p: I think this might be one of the most common problems I see when I'm working with my clients as a therapist or as a coach: the belief that if we don't know what's causing us to feel anxiety, or anger, or depression, or fill in the blank, then we can't fix it. And that brings up another problem, which is the idea of fixing these things in the first place.

I got this question from someone in my community, in regard to safety anchors, which are all about how to feel safe, how to recognize it, and how to build up the capacity to feel safe day in and day out:

q: I'm not sure they will work for me. I don't know what's triggering my anxiety.

blocks.p: He then gave me a year-by-year rundown of some of what he's been through and what he's attempted. It sounds like he's definitely putting in, quote unquote, the work. He's done everything one could ask of him. And then he says:

q: My biggest problem is I don't know what's creating this internal anxiety drive. If I don't know what it is, I can't fix it. It would seem that over the years I have created some safety spaces and recovered, but there is still some driving underneath. I felt safe running, safe at university, and then safe at a specific area. They never lasted.

blocks.p: I want to respond to a couple of pieces of this.

If we don't know what's causing the feeling, can we fix it? On the one hand, of course, knowing what's causing anxiety is super helpful. If you know that heights, or spiders, or a certain person, or just going to work causes you anxiety, it makes it a lot easier to set yourself up to decrease the amount of anxiety, if not eliminate it altogether.

If you know you're afraid of spiders, you don't go around spiders, and all of a sudden you don't have anxiety. That pretty much solves the problem, right? Does it help you grow and face your fears? No, not really. But it gets rid of the anxiety.

If you know you're anxious about going to work, I guess you could just stop going to work. Sure. But maybe you could start to identify more specifically what at work is causing you anxiety. Maybe it's not all of work. Maybe it's certain people. Maybe your cubicle or office is too cramped, and you need to declutter, and that might help reduce your anxiety. Maybe you need to get up and walk around in the middle of the day instead of being on TikTok or whatever social media platform during your break.
So if we know the context, heck yeah, it's a lot easier to address anxiety, or anger, or depression, or whatever.

blocks.h: But you don't need to know the cause

blocks.p: At the same time, no, we don't need to know what's causing it for things to get better. Say you're going to work day in and day out, and you have no idea why you feel anxious. A lot of good can come from letting yourself feel anxious, no matter the context.

If you give yourself permission to have all of your feelings, no matter what they are, that actually helps reduce the intensity of the feeling. So even though you're not aware that work is the trigger, you can still do this while you're at work:

ol: Acknowledge it. Notice that you have anxiety.
Permit it. Give it permission to be there.

Listen to what it needs. If you truly listen to what your feelings, what your body needs, it might tell you, "Get up and take a walk on your break." It might tell you, "Put the phone down, stare out the window, and breathe mindfully."

blocks.p: If you listen deeply enough, it'll tell you what it needs. So you don't really need to know what's causing it. Your body will tell you, "Here's the answer. This is what we need." And that can help to alleviate it.

The other issue in this question is what he said toward the end: some contexts helped him recover, but there's still something "driving underneath." That's a really big issue, and it's probably what brings people to the Polyvagal Theory in the first place: there's something else happening within me that I don't know how to cope with or turn off.

It's never that easy. Sometimes it is just that we're around a spider and we get triggered into anxiety. But many people have underlying anxiety always present in their system, whether they're aware of it or not. It's always there, at least at a low level, ready to be triggered. It's just kind of lingering.

That would be due to their autonomic nervous system being stuck, probably in a state of sympathetic flight activation. Even though they're not getting up and running around, the body is prepared to run around. The body is prepared to escape. It's already sympathetically driven, at least a little bit.

Then when we go to that certain environment, like work, or around that certain person, now it becomes triggered. It was already there. It was waiting, lying dormant. Now it's triggered, and we feel it, and we think, "What the heck is causing this?" That's a valid question. But it was already there. So it's not just the thing causing it.

One may always be in a state of flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, and so pinpointing a cause day to day is kind of a moot point. Of course, it has a lot to do with the past: the way we were raised, the things we've been through, culture, family, religious beliefs, everything. All of these contribute to whatever state we are stuck in, for better or worse. And that's where the question of "what's causing this?" really falls apart. It's not just one thing causing it. Now we're talking about being stuck in a state of defense, potentially for a lifetime.

The other piece I want to address, and I don't think it's nitpicky: this person, and pretty much everybody I work with in therapy and as a coach (I can't think of anyone where this wasn't true), comes to me wanting to fix how they feel.
In no way do I blame them. I fall into this thinking pattern myself. No one's immune to it. But the reality is that our feelings and emotions don't need fixing.

When I call the podcast Stuck Not Broken, I really mean it. I don't think anyone here is broken. Anyone reading, myself included, I don't think we're broken. We might be stuck at some point, but not broken. If we're broken, we need fixing. If we're stuck, then we just need to get unstuck and continue down our path in life. And that's a long road, potentially.

I don't think our emotions and our thoughts are here because we're broken in some way, or because we have some sort of illness. I don't view things that way. So when people come to me wanting to fix things, there's an obstacle there, because you're not broken.

The way you feel is, damn near 100% of the time in the people I've worked with, a direct result of your life context. Is someone born more or less likely to be anxious? Maybe. I have no way of verifying or proving that whatsoever. But every time I meet with someone and learn what they're going through and learn about their history, it makes sense. It makes sense why somebody would be stuck in a state of flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze. It makes sense why they would adopt whatever coping mechanisms they have to deal with that stuck state.

It doesn't make sense to me how we could fix something that makes complete sense. It's not broken. You're not broken. Your stuck state is there for a reason. It's normal, based on the context of your life. I don't understand what's broken about that, or what needs fixing about that.

blocks.h: Reframe fixing into validate, normalize, permit

blocks.p: So instead, let's tweak the way we think about this. People who follow my work might say, "Justin, you don't like it when people focus on thoughts as the root of the problem." Of course I agree. I don't think thoughts are the root of the problem. But here we'll use a cognitive skill, a reframe, and replace the need to be fixed with three steps:

ol: Normalize. Your feelings make sense based on the context of your life.
Permit. Give them permission to be there.

blocks.p: What I find time and time again, whether in my one-on-one client work or in the live cohorts I run, is that when we validate, normalize, and actually permit our feelings to be there instead of trying to fix them, they soften. They get, quote unquote, better. They don't go away completely. It's not a cure. But that process significantly reduces the intensity of what we're going through, again and again, and it opens up some capacity to feel it and go deeper into it, especially when combined with safety: passively, and by mindfully grounding in our safety state.
So instead of "I need fixing," it's "I'm just stuck." If you're into this polyvagal stuff like I am, that stuck message should really resonate with you. I invite you to take that reframe seriously.

If you can do that, can you validate how you feel? Just acknowledge it. Can you normalize how you feel based on the context of your life? Can you give permission to how you feel? If you can do that, especially when combined with safety, now you have the potential to listen to your body, to feel deeply what you're going through, and then to act on the underlying sensations and impulses that come along with your stuck defensive state.

This is a very high-level overview. The process of validating, normalizing, and permitting, and of feeling into your stuck defensive state, is way more involved, with a lot of pieces I can't go over here. But at a minimum, if you take one thing away: you're not broken. You're stuck, like all of us on some level. You're stuck with the potential to get unstuck, not broken and desperate for fixing.
Knowing the why of something can be really helpful. Is it necessary? No, not really.

When I work with my clients one on one, they always say, "I don't know why. I don't know why I feel this way." We always figure it out. But I tell them, "We don't need to know why. We just need to know what you feel in the present moment." We have lots to work with right there.

As we feel things in the present moment, the why of it becomes a lot clearer. Memories start to come up. Old feelings start to come up. If we can get to just what you feel in the present moment, without trying to make it go away, without judging it, without minimizing it, there's so much there to work with.
The why is still important, but it's not necessary.
